new_statements.quote: It is possible that the contrast is a matter of stress rather than in length in the case of adjectives, but this possibility has not been fully investigatied yet. [...] 2.3.2. Tones. We have established a two tone system for Rongpo, but it is difficult to find true minimal pairs to show the contrasts. These tones are high falling, marked with /»a/, and level, which is not marked in our data. [...] Zoller (1983) also established a similar system of tones in Rongpo and he called these tones high tone and mid tone, but he did not mention the tone alternation.
new_statements.citation: Sharma, Suhnu Ram. 2001. A Sketch of Rongpo Grammar. In Yasuhiko Nagano & Randy J. LaPolla (eds.), New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages (Senri Ethnological Reports 19), 195-270. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology. (Same text in LaPolla (ed.) 2001, The Tibeto-Burman Languages of Uttar Pradesh, pp. 9-72.)
new_statements.locator: §2.1.1 General features of vowels, p. 195, and §2.3.2 Tones, p. 201 (SER 19 pagination; = pp. 9 and 15 of the LaPolla UP compilation, PDF pp. 15 and 21)
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word-stress placement is given. The sketch treats Rongpo as a two-tone language (high falling vs unmarked level, with tone alternations in imperative forms) and lists only nasalization and tone as supra-segmental phonemes; the sole mention of stress is the speculation that the medial vowel-length contrast in adjectives might really be stress, left uninvestigated.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: high falling may surface as level and vice versa in certain constructions, e.g. /t»appəŋ/ 'to beat' vs imperatives /tad/, /tɛni/; /thiŋpəŋ/ 'to spread' level but imperatives /th»iŋ/, /th»iŋni/ high falling.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme level; Marcha dialect data (informant from Chinka village, Chamoli). Printed SER 19 wording differs trivially from the born-digital file ('rather than length', 'fully investigated'); SER 19 scanned renders 'falling' as 'fa11ing'.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 2001 describes the Marcha (Marchha) dialect of the Mana/Niti valleys, Chamoli (informant from Chinka village); he states Marcha and Tolcha differ only phonetically. Glottolog rong1264 = Rongpo covers both; WALS 'Marchha' (mrc) maps to rong1264. Distinct from Rangkas of Johar (LSI 'Rangkas or Saukiya Khun'), which is a separate Almora-group language. Glottolog ref 557422 ('Sharma 2003, in Thurgood & LaPolla, The Sino-Tibetan Languages, pp. 9-77') appears to be a misattributed record of the same sketch as it appears in LaPolla (ed.) 2001, The Tibeto-Burman Languages of Uttar Pradesh, pp. 9-72, not a separate work.

sources.locator: §2.1.1 General features of vowels, p. 195, and §2.3.2 Tones, p. 201 (SER 19 pagination; = pp. 9 and 15 of the LaPolla UP compilation, PDF pp. 15 and 21)
sources.note: No stress section. 2.1.1 (p. 195): adjective vowel-length contrast 'possibl[y] a matter of stress rather than length... not fully investigated yet'. 2.3 Supra-segmental phonemes (p. 201) = nasalization + two tones (high falling vs level; alternations in imperatives); Zoller 1983 reported as positing high vs mid tone. Nothing on where stress falls.

sources.citation: LaPolla, Randy J. (ed.). 2001. The Tibeto-Burman Languages of Uttar Pradesh. City University of Hong Kong, 279 pp. (pre-print compilation; contains Suhnu Ram Sharma, 'A Sketch of Rongpo Grammar', pp. 9-72, same text as the SER 19 version)
sources.note: Identical text to SER 19 version (born-digital, clean): only 'stress' mention is the speculative remark on adjective length (p. 9); supra-segmentals = nasalization + two tones (p. 15). The whole 279-page volume has no other 'stress'/'accent' hit for Rongpo.
